findings.title: Backup-code login can bypass password verification
findings.body: Password verification above this branch is skipped whenever credentials.totpCode is nonempty. The new backup-code branch takes precedence over TOTP validation, so a request containing a valid backupCode and any arbitrary nonempty totpCode authenticates without a correct password or a valid TOTP. This makes a stolen backup code sufficient to access a password-based account. Require password verification for password-based backup-code login independently of whether a totpCode was supplied.

findings.title: Backup-code consumption is not atomic
findings.body: The remaining codes are computed from the user record read earlier and then written with an unconditional update by user ID. Two concurrent requests can both validate and successfully use the same supposedly single-use code. Requests using different codes can also overwrite each other's changes, restoring a consumed code. Consume codes atomically, for example with a conditional update against the original stored value and rejection or retry when that update loses the race.

findings.title: OAuth two-factor users cannot reach backup-code recovery
findings.body: The backup-code input is only shown after twoFactorLostAccess is set by the Lost access button, but login pages with totpEmail use ExternalTotpFooter, which only offers Cancel. Consequently, Google/SAML users redirected to this two-factor screen cannot use their saved backup codes after losing their authenticator, including users who generated codes before switching their account to OAuth. The credentials provider also rejects non-CAL users when only backupCode is supplied because its identity-provider checks require totpCode. Support recovery in both the external-login footer and the corresponding server checks.
